passage_text: Red cells from a healthy donor and from a patient with pyruvate kinase deficiency were incubated with 5 mM glucose for 30 minutes, then quenched and assayed for glycolytic intermediates. Table 1 reports concentrations in nmol per mg of hemoglobin. The patient has chronic hemolytic anemia with reticulocytosis, and his red cells show a high 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate level. Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the last ATP-generating step of glycolysis.
table_data:
| Metabolite | Control red cells | Patient red cells |
|---|---|---|
| Glucose-6-phosphate | 38 | 30 |
| Phosphoenolpyruvate | 3 | 14 |
| Pyruvate | 12 | 2 |
| Lactate | 1800 | 620 |
| 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate | 4200 | 7800 |
| ATP | 1200 | 640 |
stem: Which metabolite pattern directly reflects the blocked step in this patient?

options.A: Phosphoenolpyruvate is high and pyruvate is low, because the step converting one to the other is impaired
options.B: Glucose-6-phosphate is high and lactate is low, because hexokinase is impaired
options.C: Lactate is low because lactate dehydrogenase is absent
options.D: ATP is high because glycolysis is accelerated

explanation: Pyruvate kinase converts phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate while phosphorylating ADP, so a partial deficiency backs up phosphoenolpyruvate and starves the pyruvate pool. Table 1 shows phosphoenolpyruvate rising from 3 to 14 while pyruvate falls from 12 to 2. Lactate falls as a downstream consequence, not because lactate dehydrogenase is missing.
memorize: Pyruvate kinase: phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate, generating ATP
A block backs up the substrate of the blocked step and depletes downstream products

fm.formula: phosphoenolpyruvate + ADP goes to pyruvate + ATP
fm.variables: Pyruvate kinase is the enzyme; phosphoenolpyruvate is substrate and pyruvate the product
fm.values: phosphoenolpyruvate 3 to 14 nmol/mg, pyruvate 12 to 2 nmol/mg
fm.substitution: 14/3 is about 4.7-fold higher phosphoenolpyruvate; 12 to 2 is a 6-fold fall
fm.why: Enzyme blockade raises the substrate and lowers the product of that specific reaction, which identifies the lesion
fm.no_calc: Substrate up, product down: the block sits between them

correct_rationale_plain: The substrate of pyruvate kinase accumulates while its product falls, pinpointing the blocked conversion.

wrong.B: Glucose-6-phosphate is slightly low, not high, and hexokinase blockade would raise glucose rather than lower lactate alone
wrong.C: Lactate dehydrogenase is present; lactate falls because pyruvate is scarce
wrong.D: ATP is low at 640, not high, so glycolysis is not accelerated

sc: Substrate piles up, product runs out.
mn: Block a step: behind it floods, ahead of it dries.

stem: How many net ATP molecules does one glucose molecule yield in mature red cells, which lack mitochondria?
explanation: Red cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis because they have no mitochondria. Hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1 consume two ATP, and the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps produce four, for a net of two. The NADH made at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step is reoxidized by lactate dehydrogenase, so no further ATP follows.
memorize: Anaerobic glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose
Red cells lack mitochondria, so pyruvate becomes lactate

fm.formula: net ATP = substrate-level ATP produced - ATP invested
fm.variables: Two ATP are invested at hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1; four are produced, two at phosphoglycerate kinase and two at pyruvate kinase
fm.why: Without mitochondria, the two NADH made in the cytosol cannot feed the electron transport chain, so only substrate-level phosphorylation contributes
fm.no_calc: Four made minus two spent is two net

correct_rationale_plain: Four ATP are produced and two are spent, so the anaerobic net yield is 2 ATP per glucose.

wrong.B: Four is the gross production before subtracting the two ATP invested
wrong.C: 30 is the older aerobic estimate using different phosphate-to-oxygen ratios, and red cells have no mitochondria
wrong.D: 32 is the full aerobic yield, which requires oxidative phosphorylation

mn: Red cells pay two, earn four, keep two.

stem: Why is 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate elevated in this patient, and what is its effect on hemoglobin?

options.A: It rises because ATP is high, and it tightens oxygen binding
options.B: It rises because pyruvate accumulates, and it has no effect on hemoglobin
options.C: It rises because glycolytic intermediates back up and are diverted into the bisphosphoglycerate shunt, shifting the oxygen curve right
options.D: It falls because the block prevents its synthesis, shifting the curve left

explanation: When glycolysis stalls at pyruvate kinase, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and its upstream intermediates accumulate and more is diverted to 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate by bisphosphoglycerate mutase. The extra 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate binds deoxygenated hemoglobin, stabilizes the T state, and shifts the oxygen curve right. That improves oxygen unloading even though the cell makes less ATP.
memorize: 2,3-BPG is made from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate by bisphosphoglycerate mutase
2,3-BPG stabilizes T-state hemoglobin and right-shifts the oxygen curve

fm.variables: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase makes 2,3-BPG; 2,3-BPG phosphatase removes it
fm.why: Substrate backup upstream of the block feeds the shunt, so the alternate product accumulates
fm.no_calc: Nearly double the control value, so the shunt is running harder

correct_rationale_plain: Upstream intermediates accumulate and feed the shunt, raising 2,3-BPG, which right-shifts hemoglobin and aids oxygen release.

wrong.A: ATP is low in this patient, and 2,3-BPG loosens rather than tightens oxygen binding
wrong.B: Pyruvate is low, and 2,3-BPG is a potent allosteric regulator of hemoglobin
wrong.D: The block is downstream of the shunt, so 2,3-BPG rises, not falls

sc: Block after the shunt feeds the shunt.

stem: Why does pyruvate kinase deficiency cause hemolysis?

options.A: Hemoglobin oxidizes to methemoglobin because NADPH is low
options.B: Lactate accumulates and acidifies the cell
options.C: Iron overload damages the red cell membrane
options.D: ATP falls, so the sodium-potassium pump cannot maintain cell volume and the cell ruptures

explanation: Red cells have no mitochondria and depend entirely on glycolysis for ATP. When ATP falls, the sodium-potassium ATPase slows, sodium enters, water follows, and the cell swells and lyses. The low ATP also impairs membrane remodeling, which is why splenic macrophages remove these cells.
memorize: Red-cell ATP powers the sodium-potassium ATPase
ATP depletion causes sodium and water influx, cell swelling and hemolysis

fm.formula: pump rate depends on ATP availability
fm.variables: The sodium-potassium ATPase exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions per ATP
fm.substitution: 640/1200 is about 0.53, so ATP is roughly halved
fm.why: Without enough ATP the pump cannot keep up with passive sodium leak, so osmotic water follows sodium into the cell
fm.no_calc: Half the ATP means less pump activity and a swollen cell

correct_rationale_plain: Falling ATP stalls the sodium-potassium pump, sodium and water enter, and the cell lyses.

wrong.A: NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway, and this patient's defect is in glycolysis
wrong.B: Lactate is low, not high, in this patient
wrong.C: Iron overload is a transfusion complication, not the mechanism of hemolysis here

sc: Red cell ATP equals pump equals volume control.
mn: No ATP, no pump, no shape.

stem: Sodium fluoride is added to a red-cell lysate. Which intermediate should accumulate?
explanation: Fluoride inhibits enolase, which converts 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate. The substrate of the blocked step therefore accumulates while phosphoenolpyruvate and pyruvate fall. fm.no_calc: Fluoride blocks the step into phosphoenolpyruvate, so the previous intermediate rises

stem: Which two glycolytic enzymes perform substrate-level phosphorylation?
explanation: Phosphoglycerate kinase transfers a phosphate from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP, and pyruvate kinase transfers one from phosphoenolpyruvate to ADP. Both make ATP without oxygen or a proton gradient. Hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1 do the opposite and consume ATP.

Hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1 consume ATP

fm.variables: The phosphate donor is 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate for phosphoglycerate kinase and phosphoenolpyruvate for pyruvate kinase
fm.values: two ATP per glucose from each enzyme, four total
fm.why: A high-energy phosphate is transferred directly to ADP, which does not require the electron transport chain
fm.no_calc: Two ATP-producing steps times two trioses equals four ATP

correct_rationale_plain: Phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase each transfer a high-energy phosphate to ADP, making ATP directly.

wrong.C: These dehydrogenases transfer electrons to NAD+, not phosphate to ADP

sc: ATP-making kinases: phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase.
mn: PGK and PK pay; HK and PFK charge.

stem: Arsenate is added to a red-cell lysate at a concentration that replaces phosphate in the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction. What is the net ATP yield from glucose?
explanation: Arsenate forms 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate, which hydrolyzes spontaneously without generating ATP at phosphoglycerate kinase. The two ATP invested at hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1 are still spent, and the two normally made at pyruvate kinase remain, so the net is 4 minus 2 minus 2, or zero. This is the classic arsenate uncoupling of substrate-level phosphorylation.
memorize: Arsenate uncouples glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase from ATP production
Net ATP with arsenate is zero, not two

fm.formula: net ATP = ATP made - ATP invested
fm.variables: Pyruvate kinase still makes two ATP; phosphoglycerate kinase makes none because the arsenate intermediate hydrolyzes
fm.why: The energy of the acyl phosphate is lost to spontaneous hydrolysis, so it cannot phosphorylate ADP
fm.no_calc: Two spent and only two earned downstream leaves nothing

correct_rationale_plain: Arsenate bypasses the phosphoglycerate kinase ATP step, so the two ATP invested are never recovered and the net is zero.

wrong.A: Two is the normal net yield, which requires an intact phosphoglycerate kinase step
wrong.B: Four is gross production, and arsenate removes two of those four
wrong.C: 32 is the aerobic yield and requires mitochondria, which red cells lack

sc: Arsenate steals one ATP-making step: net zero.
mn: Arsenate: arsenate, not phosphate, so the payoff evaporates.

stem: A liver cell is shifted from aerobic to anaerobic conditions. Which change in glycolysis is expected?

options.A: Lactate production rises and pyruvate is diverted from the mitochondrion
options.C: ATP yield per glucose rises to 32
options.D: Phosphofructokinase-1 is inhibited by rising ATP

explanation: Without oxygen, mitochondrial oxidation slows and cytosolic NADH cannot be reoxidized by the electron transport chain. Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+, keeping glycolysis running. ATP yield per glucose falls sharply, and AMP rises, which activates rather than inhibits phosphofructokinase-1.

Lactate fermentation yields 2 ATP per glucose, not 32

fm.values: two NADH per glucose must be reoxidized to keep glycolysis going
fm.why: Glycolysis needs a continuous NAD+ supply, and without oxygen only the lactate reaction can provide it
fm.no_calc: Each glucose needs two NAD+ regenerated, so two lactate are made

correct_rationale_plain: Lack of oxygen forces pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.

stem: Which enzyme sets the rate of glycolysis in liver and is the main site of its regulation?
explanation: Phosphofructokinase-1 catalyzes the committed and most regulated step of glycolysis, converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. It is activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate. Hexokinase is regulated too, but in liver glucokinase handles glucose phosphorylation and the pathway's flux control sits at phosphofructokinase-1.
memorize: Phosphofructokinase-1 is the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis
PFK-1: activated by AMP and F2,6BP, inhibited by ATP and citrate

fm.variables: PFK-1 is the enzyme; ATP is both substrate and allosteric inhibitor
fm.values: not needed; regulation defines the step
fm.why: The step is the first committed reaction after glucose entry, so regulating it controls flux without wasting intermediates
fm.no_calc: Look for the step that commits the sugar to glycolysis

correct_rationale_plain: PFK-1 makes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the committed step, and is controlled by ATP, AMP, citrate and F2,6BP.

wrong.A: Hexokinase sets entry of glucose into the cell but is not the main flux-controlling step in liver
wrong.B: Pyruvate kinase is regulated but catalyzes a later, noncommitted step
wrong.D: Lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+ and is not rate-limiting

mn: PFK-1: the gate that commits glucose.

stem: How does a high ATP/AMP ratio affect phosphofructokinase-1?

options.A: It activates the enzyme by increasing its affinity for fructose-6-phosphate
options.B: It inhibits the enzyme by lowering its affinity for fructose-6-phosphate
options.C: It has no effect because ATP is a substrate, not a regulator
options.D: It converts the enzyme into a covalent phosphorylated form

explanation: ATP binds an allosteric site distinct from the active site and shifts phosphofructokinase-1 toward the T state, raising the Km for fructose-6-phosphate. AMP reverses this by binding the R state, which is why the ATP/AMP ratio signals energy status. The inhibition is a classic feedback control, not a covalent modification.
memorize: ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of PFK-1 and raises Km for fructose-6-phosphate
AMP is an allosteric activator and reverses ATP inhibition

fm.formula: v = Vmax[S]/(Km,app + [S]), with Km,app rising as ATP binds
fm.variables: S is fructose-6-phosphate; ATP binds an allosteric inhibitory site
fm.values: high ATP raises Km,app; AMP lowers it
fm.substitution: not needed; the effect is a Km shift, not a Vmax change
fm.why: A greater Km at the same substrate concentration lowers fractional saturation of the enzyme, slowing flux
fm.no_calc: More ATP means a higher Km for F6P, so velocity falls

correct_rationale_plain: ATP binds an allosteric site and lowers PFK-1 affinity for fructose-6-phosphate, slowing glycolysis when energy is plentiful.

wrong.C: ATP serves as both substrate and allosteric inhibitor at a separate site
wrong.D: Covalent regulation of PFK-1 is not the mechanism here; the change is allosteric and immediate

sc: High ATP equals low PFK-1 affinity.
mn: ATP fills the tank and closes the pump.

options.A: It accelerates because fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates phosphofructokinase-1 and opposes ATP inhibition

stem: Glucagon acts on the liver during fasting. What is its effect on glycolysis?

options.A: It raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and accelerates glycolysis
options.B: It activates pyruvate kinase by dephosphorylation
options.C: It has no effect on liver glycolysis because glucagon acts only on muscle
options.D: It lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibits glycolysis while favoring gluconeogenesis

explanation: Glucagon raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2. The phosphatase activity then dominates, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, and phosphofructokinase-1 loses its activator, so glycolysis slows. The same signal inactivates pyruvate kinase by phosphorylation, shunting carbon toward glucose production.

Insulin does the opposite: raises F2,6BP and activates glycolysis

fm.substitution: not needed; the direction is set by the phosphatase activity
fm.why: Removing the activator lowers PFK-1 saturation at any given fructose-6-phosphate concentration, reducing flux

correct_rationale_plain: Glucagon lowers F2,6BP through PKA, so PFK-1 slows and the liver makes glucose instead of burning it.

wrong.A: That is the insulin response, not glucagon
wrong.B: Glucagon promotes phosphorylation of pyruvate kinase, which inhibits it
wrong.C: Glucagon acts on liver and has little effect on muscle glycolysis

sc: Glucagon equals low F2,6BP equals glycolysis off.

passage_text: Red cells from a healthy donor and from a patient with pyruvate kinase deficiency were incubated with 5 mM glucose for 30 minutes, then quenched and assayed for glycolytic intermediates. Table 1 reports concentrations in nmol per mg of hemoglobin. The patient has chronic hemolytic anemia with reticulocytosis, and his red cells show a high 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate level. Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the last ATP-generating step of glycolysis.
table_data:
| Metabolite | Control red cells | Patient red cells |
|---|---|---|
| Glucose-6-phosphate | 38 | 30 |
| Phosphoenolpyruvate | 3 | 14 |
| Pyruvate | 12 | 2 |
| Lactate | 1800 | 620 |
| 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate | 4200 | 7800 |
| ATP | 1200 | 640 |
stem: What is the main function of the pentose phosphate pathway in red cells?

options.A: Generating ATP for the sodium-potassium pump
options.B: Producing NADPH to maintain reduced glutathione and protect hemoglobin from oxidation

explanation: The oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway reduces NADP+ to NADPH, which keeps glutathione reduced through glutathione reductase. Reduced glutathione detoxifies peroxides and protects hemoglobin and membrane lipids from oxidative damage. The pathway makes no ATP, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is its rate-limiting enzyme.
memorize: Pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate, not ATP
G6PD deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis

fm.formula: glucose-6-phosphate + 2 NADP+ goes to ribulose-5-phosphate + 2 NADPH + CO2
fm.variables: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is rate-limiting; NADPH is the reducing output
fm.why: NADPH donates electrons to glutathione reductase, replenishing the reduced glutathione pool
fm.no_calc: Count NADPH, not ATP: two per glucose-6-phosphate

correct_rationale_plain: The pathway supplies NADPH, which regenerates reduced glutathione and prevents oxidative damage in red cells.

wrong.A: The pathway produces no ATP; red cells get ATP from glycolysis
wrong.C: Lactate is made by lactate dehydrogenase in glycolysis
wrong.D: 2,3-BPG comes from the glycolytic shunt at 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate

stem: Using 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 ATP per FADH2, and the malate-aspartate shuttle, what is the total ATP yield from complete oxidation of one glucose?
explanation: Glycolysis gives 4 substrate-level ATP and 2 cytosolic NADH; pyruvate dehydrogenase gives 2 NADH; the two turns of the citric acid cycle give 6 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 2 GTP. That is 10 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 4 ATP equivalents. Using 2.5 and 1.5 ATP per reduced carrier gives 25 plus 3 plus 4, or 32.
memorize: Full glucose oxidation: 10 NADH, 2 FADH2, 4 ATP equivalents
2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2 give a total of 32

fm.variables: NADH count includes 2 cytosolic, 2 from pyruvate dehydrogenase and 6 from the citric acid cycle; FADH2 comes only from succinate dehydrogenase
fm.why: Each carrier feeds a defined number of protons into the gradient, and the ATP synthase converts that gradient into a fixed ATP yield
fm.no_calc: Ten NADH give 25, two FADH2 give 3, and four direct ATP make 32

correct_rationale_plain: Ten NADH give 25 ATP, two FADH2 give 3, and four substrate-level ATP bring the total to 32.

wrong.A: 30 uses a glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, which delivers cytosolic NADH as FADH2 and loses two ATP
wrong.B: 28 double-counts the shuttle penalty and drops one citric acid cycle turn
wrong.D: 36 comes from the older 3 and 2 ATP per carrier convention

sc: Count carriers first, then multiply by 2.5 and 1.5.
mn: Ten and two and four: 25 plus 3 plus 4.

stem: Why does one glycosyl unit from glycogen yield one more net ATP than free glucose during anaerobic glycolysis?

options.A: The hexokinase step is bypassed, so no ATP is spent to phosphorylate the sugar
options.B: Glycogen phosphorylase makes two ATP directly
options.C: Glycogenysis produces NADPH instead of NADH

explanation: Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-phosphate, which is converted to glucose-6-phosphate without using ATP. Free glucose must be phosphorylated by hexokinase at a cost of one ATP, so the glycogen-derived unit nets three ATP instead of two. The rest of glycolysis is unchanged.
memorize: Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-phosphate, skipping hexokinase
Anaerobic glycogen yield: 3 ATP per glycosyl unit versus 2 for glucose

fm.variables: Glucose invests 1 ATP at hexokinase; glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen does not
fm.values: 4 produced, 1 invested for glycogen; 4 produced, 2 invested for glucose
fm.why: Phosphorolysis already yields a phosphorylated sugar, so the cell avoids the hexokinase investment
fm.no_calc: Skip one ATP payment and the net rises by one

correct_rationale_plain: Glycogen gives glucose-1-phosphate, so hexokinase is skipped and the net gain is one ATP higher.

wrong.B: Glycogen phosphorylase uses inorganic phosphate and makes glucose-1-phosphate, not ATP
wrong.C: Glycogenolysis yields glucose-6-phosphate, and NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway
wrong.D: Pyruvate kinase is still required to make the last two ATP
